subtopics.title: Relative motion, signed graphs and piecewise meetings — advanced construction pilot
subtopics.learning_goal: Translate positions, observers and stagewise movement into valid signed models, and reject physically invalid encounter times.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Identify the frame and compose velocities correctly when a walker moves on a moving walkway; defend the chosen model.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: Declare east-positive ground frame; add the walker's velocity relative to the walkway to walkway velocity relative to the ground; compute closing rate and check direction.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Select a moving-frame velocity-composition model over a single stationary-frame velocity statement.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate two relative-velocity statements into a signed ground-frame description.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: The model choice must precede a closing-rate calculation, then an encounter check.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: One subtraction after velocity composition; simple arithmetic is not what carries the proposed demand.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Opposite directions and relative-velocity sign require a genuine condition check.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Construct signed velocity-time representation from position-time data and distinguish the invariant displacement from distance.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: Calculate signed slopes of consecutive position-time intervals, plot corresponding velocity steps, integrate signed areas and verify original endpoints.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Choose correct piecewise slope interpretation instead of treating position as speed.

representation_translation.evidence: Transform a measured position table to velocity segments with sign, scale and interval boundaries preserved.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Translate the intervals, then recover signed area and back-compare final minus initial position.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Arithmetic is routine and does not carry this representation challenge.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: A zero-slope plateau and reversed direction require independent interpretation.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Recognize that the first-stage meeting time is outside its interval and construct a valid post-reversal or post-delay encounter model.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: Set up the first-stage equations, reject the mathematically valid out-of-domain root, write a second interval model, solve and substitute both positions.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Select and switch the correct piecewise model after a physical reversal or delayed start.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate a motion timeline into separate position expressions with valid domains.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Test the candidate time, repair the model and verify the meeting under its own interval.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: At least two linear meeting equations with interval-dependent constants.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: An algebraically correct first-stage root can be physically invalid and must be rejected.

science_records.claim: For a one-dimensional motion, displacement is final position minus initial position and distance is total path length.
science_records.law_or_model: signed one-dimensional position and cumulative distance
assumptions: One fixed coordinate axis is declared
A common reference frame for all positions
conditions_and_limits: The absolute value of net displacement never exceeds path length.
A coordinate reversal changes displacement sign but does not alter path distance.
science_records.units_and_signs: x and Δx in m, east positive unless specified; distance is nonnegative.

science_records.claim: For two bodies' velocities measured in the same non-rotating reference frame, relative velocity along one axis is the signed difference.
science_records.law_or_model: v(B/A) = vB − vA; Galilean composition in classical one-dimensional kinematics
assumptions: The compared velocities are signed on the same axis
Speeds sufficiently slow that elementary Galilean composition applies
The frame is suitably inertial for subsequent Newtonian force reasoning
conditions_and_limits: Relative velocities stated in different intermediate frames must be composed in order.
Do not add unsigned speeds automatically or infer meeting time without initial separation.
science_records.units_and_signs: Signed velocities in m/s, signed east positive.

science_records.claim: On a velocity-time graph, the signed area over a time interval is displacement, whereas total distance sums the magnitudes of segment contributions.
science_records.law_or_model: piecewise v–t area and x–t slope
assumptions: The graphed quantities use a fixed coordinate system
Time interval is partitioned at genuine changes of velocity law
conditions_and_limits: Signed area is not automatically positive distance.
Vertical velocity jumps are idealizations; actual finite force implies finite-time change.
science_records.units_and_signs: Velocity m/s; time s; signed area m; positive and negative velocities are directions.

science_records.claim: Each position formula applies only over the interval whose motion conditions define it.
science_records.law_or_model: piecewise constant-velocity motion and interval-filtered intersections
assumptions: Correct start times and initial positions are known
Each interval's velocity law is valid only within declared bounds
conditions_and_limits: A solution outside its interval is inadmissible even if the algebra is correct.
After a stop, reversal or delayed departure, use a new position expression with continuity at the boundary.
science_records.units_and_signs: Global clock t in s; positions m; each segment retains signed velocity m/s.

core1a.phenomenon: Two moving observers can assign different velocities to the same object, while a mathematical encounter time may fail because the motion model changes.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A position has meaning only relative to a frame and an axis. A journey also has a temporal structure: the physical model for a moving segment cannot be applied after a stop or reversal. Work progressively from signed positions to velocity and acceleration, convert graphs into physical displacement using signed areas, then check the domain of each equation when constructing multi-stage meetings. The reading-first textbook presents each component with a figure, derivation, model limitation and worked check; the advanced inference is rejecting an algebraically valid but physically inadmissible interval and rebuilding the correct motion model.

derivation_steps.action: Declare observer, object, axis and global time before assigning signs.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Relative position and velocity are only well-defined after fixing the measurement frame and coordinate direction.

derivation_steps.action: Translate each position segment into a signed velocity (slope) and verify by graph area.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Velocity is the rate of position change; integrating a constant signed velocity across a segment gives that segment's displacement.

derivation_steps.action: Derive the encounter time within the first valid interval and test it against the interval bounds.
derivation_steps.why_valid: An equation inherits the domain of the motion conditions from which it was constructed; an out-of-domain root is inadmissible.

derivation_steps.action: Construct the second interval's position law continuously from its boundary and re-solve the encounter.
derivation_steps.why_valid: The object's position does not jump merely because it changes speed or direction at the transition.

model_limits: Elementary constant-velocity segment equations are not correct over an interval of continuously changing velocity.
A graph's signed area gives displacement, not necessarily total distance.
Relative velocity subtraction requires consistent frames and sign conventions.
A valid equation root still requires the event to fall within that equation's physical interval.

progressive_examples.problem: A traveller walks 80 m east, then 30 m west in 20 s. Find displacement and distance.
progressive_examples.reasoning: With east positive, displacement is +80−30=+50 m; distance is 80+30=110 m. Average velocity is +2.5 m/s and average speed 5.5 m/s.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Distance ≥ magnitude of displacement; units and signed direction are consistent.

progressive_examples.problem: For 4 s a car has v=+3 m/s, then for 3 s v=−1 m/s. Determine graph area and total path length.
progressive_examples.reasoning: Signed area gives +12−3=+9 m displacement; total distance is 12+3=15 m.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Signed displacement is smaller in magnitude than distance and matches the change in endpoint position.

progressive_examples.problem: A moves east from x=0 at 4 m/s for 4 s then stops; B starts x=40 m and moves west at 3 m/s. When do they meet?
progressive_examples.reasoning: For 0≤t≤4, 4t=40−3t yields t=40/7≈5.71 s, outside its validity. After 4 s A is at x=16, so 16=40−3t gives t=8 s and position x=16 m.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Both actual position models give x=16 at t=8; the first-stage root is rejected as out-of-domain.

figures.reasoning_step: Distinguish path distance and signed displacement
figures.scene_description: Walk from x0 to x80 and back to x50 on east-positive axis, as drawn in textbook PH01 section 1.

figures.reasoning_step: Interpret signed area below velocity-time axis
figures.scene_description: Velocity +3 m/s for 4 s then −1 m/s for 3 s, with signed area colored by sign, as drawn in section 5.

misconception.wrong_model: Treat an algebraic meeting time as valid even when its first-stage motion assumption has ended.
misconception.diagnostic: If equation xA=4t is valid only for t≤4 s, is the solution t=5.71 s a real first-stage meeting?
misconception.repair: Reject the out-of-domain candidate, construct xA=16 for t≥4, then recompute and verify both positions.

exit_check.task: An object moves +3 m/s for 2 s then −1 m/s for 4 s. Compare displacement and distance and explain signs.
exit_check.reasoning: Velocity-time signed areas add for displacement; absolute lengths add for distance.

core1b.fresh_task: A moving walkway travels east at 2 m/s. A person walks west at 3 m/s relative to the walkway. At time zero another person is at x=−20 m and walks east at 1 m/s on the ground. Formulate the ground-frame velocities, determine whether and when they meet, and justify each sign.
core1b.protected_work: Identify the frame and compose velocities correctly when a walker moves on a moving walkway; defend the chosen model.

stages.predict: Predict whether ground-frame velocity has the same sign as the walker's relative-walkway velocity.
stages.attempt: A moving walkway travels east at 2 m/s. A person walks west at 3 m/s relative to the walkway. At time zero another person is at x=−20 m and walks east at 1 m/s on the ground. Formulate the ground-frame velocities, determine whether and when they meet, and justify each sign.
stages.reconstruct: The walkway person's ground velocity is 2−3=−1 m/s. Their x starts at 0, so xA=−t. Ground walker B has xB=−20+t. Equality gives −t=−20+t; t=10 s, meeting at x=−10 m. Confirm the first walker moves west although the walkway moves east.
stages.diagnose: Compare the saved sign choice with the actual ground-frame velocity. Did the learner add speed magnitudes, ignore the walkway, or merely err arithmetically?
stages.repair: Rebuild the velocity diagram on a single east-positive axis, then recompute the encounter and check positions.
stages.boundary_test: If the walkway speeds up to +4 m/s with the person's walk still −3 m/s relative to the walkway, which body is faster eastward and can the same initial geometry produce a meeting?

core1b.fresh_task: A kayak moves east at 4 m/s relative to the water; the current carries the water west at 1 m/s relative to shore. Another craft starts 24 m behind the kayak and travels east at 5 m/s relative to shore. Determine the kayak's shore velocity and overtaking time, stating the frame for every number.
core1b.protected_work: Identify the frame and compose velocities correctly when a walker moves on a moving walkway; defend the chosen model.

stages.predict: Predict which motion looks eastbound to an observer moving west.
stages.attempt: A kayak moves east at 4 m/s relative to the water; the current carries the water west at 1 m/s relative to shore. Another craft starts 24 m behind the kayak and travels east at 5 m/s relative to shore. Determine the kayak's shore velocity and overtaking time, stating the frame for every number.
stages.reconstruct: Kayak velocity relative shore is +4−1=+3 m/s. The rear craft gains at +5−3=+2 m/s, so it covers the 24 m gap in 12 s. This is overtaking, not head-on motion; using 5+3 would confuse the directions.
stages.diagnose: Check whether frame labels or the signed closing rate were wrong; distinguish that from a division slip.
stages.repair: Compose water-relative and shore-relative velocities on one signed number line; use relative closing velocity.
stages.boundary_test: What if the rear craft moves at only +2 m/s relative to shore? Explain whether it can overtake.

core1b.fresh_task: A device reports positions at times t=(0,2,5,7) seconds as x=(0,6,6,0) metres. Draw the piecewise velocity-time graph, state displacement and total distance, and verify by integrating signed graph areas.
core1b.protected_work: Construct signed velocity-time representation from position-time data and distinguish the invariant displacement from distance.

stages.predict: Without drawing, predict whether a return to the initial position can coexist with a positive total distance.
stages.attempt: A device reports positions at times t=(0,2,5,7) seconds as x=(0,6,6,0) metres. Draw the piecewise velocity-time graph, state displacement and total distance, and verify by integrating signed graph areas.
stages.reconstruct: Slopes are +3 m/s from 0–2 s, 0 from 2–5 s, and −3 m/s from 5–7 s. Signed areas +6, 0, −6 produce net displacement 0 m, consistent with final x−initial x. Distance is 6+0+6=12 m. The plateau in position means rest, not zero displacement accumulated earlier.
stages.diagnose: Compare first answer: was slope confused with graph height, did the learner disregard the negative segment, or was it an arithmetic slip?
stages.repair: Mark each interval, calculate signed slope, then draw three velocity steps and use reverse translation to position.
stages.boundary_test: If the final position changes to +2 m while earlier samples stay fixed, which velocity segment and which signed area change?

core1b.fresh_task: An elevator's recorded vertical positions (up positive) are t=(0,3,6,8) s and y=(5,−1,−1,3) m. Construct a velocity-time diagram, calculate the net displacement and total distance, and explain the level section.
core1b.protected_work: Construct signed velocity-time representation from position-time data and distinguish the invariant displacement from distance.

stages.predict: Which segments have negative velocity when an object crosses the origin?
stages.attempt: An elevator's recorded vertical positions (up positive) are t=(0,3,6,8) s and y=(5,−1,−1,3) m. Construct a velocity-time diagram, calculate the net displacement and total distance, and explain the level section.
stages.reconstruct: From 0–3 s, Δy=−6 m and v=−2 m/s; 3–6 s is stationary v=0; 6–8 s, Δy=+4 m and v=+2 m/s. Net displacement is −2 m, equal to 3−5. Total distance is 6+4=10 m.
stages.diagnose: Was the initial height incorrectly assumed zero? Did the learner treat the stationary segment as reversal?
stages.repair: Use slope per interval, back-integrate the velocity steps, and compare against the original y values.
stages.boundary_test: Shift every recorded position upward by 10 m. Predict how the velocity graph and displacement change.

core1b.fresh_task: Train A leaves x=0 eastbound at 6 m/s for exactly 3 s, then reverses and travels west at 2 m/s. Train B begins at x=36 m and continuously travels west at 4 m/s. At what time and position do they meet? Explicitly reject any invalid candidate.
core1b.protected_work: Recognize that the first-stage meeting time is outside its interval and construct a valid post-reversal or post-delay encounter model.

stages.predict: Predict whether two trains can meet after one reverses direction even if the first-stage meeting calculation looks too late.
stages.attempt: Train A leaves x=0 eastbound at 6 m/s for exactly 3 s, then reverses and travels west at 2 m/s. Train B begins at x=36 m and continuously travels west at 4 m/s. At what time and position do they meet? Explicitly reject any invalid candidate.
stages.reconstruct: During 0≤t≤3, xA=6t and xB=36−4t, so t=3.6 s would be the meeting time if this first-stage model continued, but it does not. At t=3, A is at x=18 and reverses: xA=18−2(t−3)=24−2t. Set 24−2t=36−4t, giving t=6 s and x=12 m. Both expressions apply after t=3 and agree.
stages.diagnose: Identify whether the learner failed to test the first candidate against t≤3, extended the wrong position expression, or changed velocity without preserving position continuity.
stages.repair: Write a timeline with the reversal at t=3, start the second position model from x=18, and substitute the final meeting time into both trajectories.
stages.boundary_test: What changes if B's westward speed drops to 1 m/s? Analyze separation and signs after A reverses before assuming a meeting exists.

core1b.fresh_task: Cyclist A starts at x=0 and rides east at 4 m/s from t=0. Cyclist B is at x=30 m and remains at rest until t=2 s, then rides west at 3 m/s. At which global time do they meet? Verify both time intervals.
core1b.protected_work: Recognize that the first-stage meeting time is outside its interval and construct a valid post-reversal or post-delay encounter model.

stages.predict: Can delaying departure change which interval contains a meeting?
stages.attempt: Cyclist A starts at x=0 and rides east at 4 m/s from t=0. Cyclist B is at x=30 m and remains at rest until t=2 s, then rides west at 3 m/s. At which global time do they meet? Verify both time intervals.
stages.reconstruct: For 0≤t≤2, A is at x=4t≤8 and B remains at x=30, so no meeting. For t≥2, B has x=30−3(t−2)=36−3t. Equating 4t=36−3t gives t=36/7≈5.14 s, after the departure time. Meeting position is x=144/7≈20.57 m, matching B's expression.
stages.diagnose: Did the learner start B's clock at t=0 rather than t=2, or fail to distinguish waiting and moving stages?
stages.repair: Create a global clock, enforce continuity at t=2, and solve only within the correct segment.
stages.boundary_test: If B never departs, when does A reach x=30? Explain why this limit is not found by simply setting B's moving speed to zero while retaining the same start assumption.
